eminent

EM-ih-nent — starts like 'emperor'; an eminent person stands out like royalty in their field. Note: eminent (famous) is easy to mix up with imminent (about to happen) — they look and sound alike but mean very different things. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Eminent is famous and respected within a particular field or profession.

An eminent panel of judges, each a leader in their field, was invited to evaluate the science fair finalists.

Example

A researcher spends forty years studying a rare disease, publishes hundreds of papers, and trains dozens of doctors around the world, becoming so eminent in her field that the World Health Organization asks her to advise on how to respond to future outbreaks.

That level of respect within a field -- so deep that world organizations seek your advice -- is what makes someone eminent. Unlike 'famous,' which can apply to anyone widely known, eminent specifically implies deep respect earned through real accomplishment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distinguished: Distinguished means honored and respected for real achievement — a distinguished judge has earned formal esteem. Eminent is similar but adds standing within a specific field: an eminent chemist is the one other chemists look up to. Neither word is a measure of how many strangers know your face.

renowned: Renowned means widely known and admired — fame that has spread far and wide, even to people who could not name your achievements. Eminent points the other way: deep respect inside a particular field or profession, even if the wider public has never heard of you.

illustrious: Illustrious means famous for great achievements, with a glow of glory attached — an illustrious career, an illustrious dynasty. It praises the achievements themselves, while eminent emphasizes the respect a person commands within their own field.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unknown: not known or recognized by others

obscure: not well known; hard to notice

Where it sits · how large the reputation has grown

notable → eminent → legendary

notable vs. eminent: Notable is weaker than eminent — something notable is simply worth mentioning, while eminent describes someone widely and deeply respected within their field.

legendary vs. eminent: Legendary can feel even bigger than eminent: eminent describes real, earned respect, but legendary suggests a reputation so large it borders on myth.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e- (ex-): out (Latin)

root — -min-: to project, to jut out (Latin (eminere))

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together: Latin eminere combined e- ('out') with a root meaning 'to project or jut,' and the suffix -ent turns it into an adjective -- 'jutting out.' Someone eminent literally stands out from the crowd, which is why the word means famous and respected.

Use the root in a new word: prominent: Before the quiz, she made flashcards for every prominent figure in the chapter.
